explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ahaziah, king of Samaria, tells his messengers, “Go inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this injury.” He fell through a lattice, and his first move is to ask a god of Ekron. I've been in a drawer, and even I know you ask the right One.

explanations.answer: Elijah the prophet of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Elijah is the man who stops the messengers, not the one they're sent to. Ahaziah, king of Samaria, instructs them to “inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.” Elijah, the man of God, only shows up when the angel of the LORD sends him up the road to meet them. Ahaziah was never planning on knocking at Elijah's door.

Dagon is a real name in the Bible, so I see why it jumped out. He's the god whose temple the Philistines had in Ashdod (1 Samuel 5:2). But Ahaziah, king of Samaria, names a different god and a different city. He sends his messengers to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.

explanations.answer: Is there no God in Israel
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The angel of the LORD tells Elijah the Tishbite to ask, “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?” Elijah doesn't ask where they're headed or who sent them. He asks the one question that points straight at the problem. And that question is going to come back around again.

Moab is in this chapter, friend, but only in the very first verse, where it rebels against Israel. It's not part of the question the angel of the LORD hands Elijah. The question is about God in Israel and about Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Ahaziah's troubles with Moab never come up on that road.

explanations.answer: Who sent you down this road
explanations.explanation: That's a fair question to ask a traveler, baker, but it isn't the one Elijah gets. We already know who sent them, because the king did. The angel of the LORD tells Elijah to ask, “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are on your way to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?” It's less about the road and more about where they're heading.

Yes, and the LORD says it plainly: “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” Ahaziah asked a god of Ekron for good news. He got the truth from the LORD, through Elijah, on the road. That's the kind of answer you can't get anywhere else.

explanations.answer: He will heal in seven days
explanations.explanation: I wish I could hand the king a nice timeline, but the LORD doesn't. There's no seven days in this passage at all. What the LORD says is, “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.”

Moab rebelled against Israel back in verse 1, so it's easy to see why it's still on your mind. But the LORD's message to Ahaziah has nothing to say about Moab. It's about the bed he's lying on, and he will not get up from it. The LORD says, “You will surely die.”

That's not how the story goes, friend. The messengers keep nothing to themselves. When the king asks why they're back, they tell him the whole thing, including the man's question and his words, “You will surely die.” They even repeat the part about Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, right to the king's face.

That's right, baker. The messengers hold nothing back. They tell the king that a man came up to meet them and said, “Go back to the king who sent you and tell him that this is what the LORD says…” Then they pass along every word, down to “You will surely die.” Whatever the king is about to feel, they delivered the message in full.

He sure can. The messengers say, “He was a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist.” And the king doesn't even blink. He answers, “It was Elijah the Tishbite.” Two details, and he's got a name.

Ahaziah, king of Samaria, needs very little to go on. The messengers say, “He was a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist.” The king answers right away, “It was Elijah the Tishbite.” That's a whole name from two details, and I can't even find my own keys with two details.

That's the message. The captain goes up to Elijah, who is sitting on top of a hill, and says, “Man of God, the king declares, ‘Come down!’” He calls Elijah a man of God, then hands him an order from the king. Remember that, because those two things don't sit together well.

Leaving Israel isn't part of this at all, friend. The captain's message is short: “Man of God, the king declares, ‘Come down!’” The king wants Elijah off that hill and brought to him. He doesn't send a word about leaving the land.
It's actually the opposite, baker. The king isn't telling Elijah to keep his distance. He sends a captain and fifty men up the hill with the order, “Come down!” Ahaziah wants Elijah close, not far.

You caught it. The second captain says, “Come down at once!” and Elijah answers, “If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” That's exactly what he said to the first captain. The only change is on the king's side, where the order gets louder.

This time the words really are the same. The text says, “Again Elijah replied, ‘If I am a man of God, may fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.’” That line comes out the same both times. Only the king's order changed, when it went from “Come down!” to “Come down at once!”

explanations.answer: The fire of God consumes them
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. After Elijah speaks, “the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” It's a heavy moment, and I'll say that once and plainly. It also shows that Elijah was speaking for God, not for himself.

explanations.answer: They run back down the hill
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets a head start in this one, friend. The text doesn't give the second captain and his men a chance to run. It says, “the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” It's a heavy moment, and the story doesn't hurry past it.

explanations.answer: The king calls them back home
explanations.explanation: No messenger from the king reaches them, baker. The king isn't in this scene at all, since he's back in his bed in Samaria. The text says, “the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.” This is a heavy part of the story, and it happens fast.

explanations.answer: He falls on his knees and begs
explanations.explanation: That's him. The third captain goes up, “fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him.” No orders this time, no “Come down!” at all. I think this captain did the math on the first two and decided to try something different.

explanations.answer: He orders Elijah down at once
explanations.explanation: That was the second captain's line, friend. The third captain does something very different. He “fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him.” He comes up asking, not telling.

explanations.answer: He offers Elijah a royal gift
explanations.explanation: No gift shows up in this scene, baker. The third captain hands over nothing from the king. What he does is “fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him.” The only thing he brings with him up that hill is a plea.

explanations.answer: That his life and his men's would be spared
explanations.explanation: That's what he's after. He says, “Man of God, may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight.” Then he adds, “But now may my life be precious in your sight.” He points to what happened to the first two captains, and he asks for his life and his men's lives.

explanations.answer: That the king would be healed of his injury
explanations.explanation: The king's injury doesn't come up in the captain's plea, friend. His words are all about himself and his men: “may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight.” He has just heard that fire consumed the first two captains. His request is for lives to be precious, not for anything to be healed.

explanations.answer: That Elijah would leave the land of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's not in his plea, baker. He doesn't ask Elijah to go anywhere. He begs, “may my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours please be precious in your sight.” It's a plea to be spared, said on his knees.

Yes, afraid. The angel of the LORD says to Elijah, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.” That's a lot of men and a lot of fire behind this moment, and the angel tells Elijah to go down anyway. I think that's a comfort, baker, because the LORD is the one giving the word to go.

I can see why this one is tempting, but shame isn't in the angel's message. The angel of the LORD says, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.” The word is afraid. Elijah is told to go down, and he doesn't need to fear this captain.

Jealousy never comes up in this scene, friend. The angel of the LORD tells Elijah, “Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him.” The word is afraid. And Elijah gets up and goes down with the captain to the king.

That's not what happens, baker. The word Elijah brings is, “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” And that's how it goes. The text says, “So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken.”

That's right. Elijah tells the king, “You will not get up from the bed on which you are lying. You will surely die.” And the king doesn't get up. The text says, “So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken.” When the LORD says it, it happens.

That's him. Ahaziah had no son, so Jehoram takes the throne of Israel after him. Now here's the part that tangles people up. There's another Jehoram too, the son of Jehoshaphat, who reigns over Judah, and the text uses his reign to mark the year. Same name, two kings, and I still can't keep two cookie cutters straight on a busy day.

Jehu does become king of Israel, but later (2 Kings 9:13). He's not the one who comes right after Ahaziah. The text says that since Ahaziah had no son, Jehoram succeeded him. So the name you want starts with Jeho, but it's Jehoram and not Jehu.

Jehoshaphat is in this passage, but he isn't taking over for Ahaziah. He's the father of the other Jehoram, the one who reigns over Judah. The text only uses him to mark the year when the Jehoram of Israel takes the throne. It says Ahaziah had no son, so Jehoram succeeded him.
